title: TTFB sawtooth alignment probe and response diary
body:
Summary:
We observed an intermittent, sawtooth-pattern TTFB (time-to-first-byte) oscillation affecting hosted API endpoints serving streaming sessions. Effect window was ~08:13–09:04 PT on 2026-05-11. Impact: elevated TTFB p95 rising from baseline ~120ms to 2.1s in recurring 30–90s cycles for ~15% of sessions, causing a subset of streaming clients to time out and surface 5xx errors. Severity: escalated to P0 because customer-facing latency SLO violations and a handful of escalations from high-revenue tenants.

Detection & alerts:
- First alert at 08:15 PT: p95 TTFB dashboard cross-threshold (pager).
- Pager rotation: primary oncall (Emma C.), secondary (Rajiv K.).
- Console: streaming session errors increased by +34% vs baseline (08:00–08:10).
- Early suspicion: either edge connection churn or upstream service backpressure.

Timeline (key events):
- 08:13 PT: earliest anomalous spike observed in synthetic probe (eu-west-1).
- 08:15 PT: automated pager fired (p95 TTFB > 1.5s). Primary acknowledged at 08:16.
- 08:18 PT: quick triage — edge-proxy queue depth spiked on a subset of hosts.
- 08:22 PT: rolled short-term mitigations: (a) temporarily increased acceptor thread pool on affected nodes; (b) enabled additional backpressure metrics stream to logs.
- 08:29 PT: partial improvement but oscillation persisted. Saw repeated ramp->drop pattern every ~45s.
- 08:36 PT: identified correlation with KV-cache lease renewals and a specific prefix hot-sweep job executing on the same shard.
- 08:40 PT: disabled the hot-sweep job on the problematic shard and moved it to lower-priority queue; immediate improvement in many nodes.
- 08:45 PT: traffic rebalanced across the region, p95 returned to ~180–220ms but intermittent spikes remained at low amplitude.
- 09:04 PT: declared incident under control.

What we measured / observability notes:
- p50/p95/p99 TTFB series (attached to dashboard): baseline p95 ~120ms, incident peak p95 ~2.1s, p99 peaks ~4.0s.
- Edge acceptor queue length on affected hosts oscillated in lockstep with TTFB sawtooth.
- KV-lease renewal latency spiked from ~8ms to ~300ms during sweep events.
- Streaming session churn: sessions reconnected with partial content and triggered 5xx on some clients that enforce strict TTFB thresholds.

Immediate mitigations executed:
1) Disabled hot-sweep job on the shard (08:40). Rationale: sweep was causing synchronous KV operations and blocking acceptor loop for some hosts.
2) Increased acceptor-thread pool temporarily (+50%) on three hosts that showed high queueing (08:22). Outcome: reduced queue tail but did not stop oscillation alone.
3) Applied short-lived configuration change to edge-proxy to favor fast-path token routing to unaffected hosts (08:27). This reduced the fraction of impacted sessions.
4) Adjusted client-side stream timeout thresholds for a small subset of enterprise tenants (with consent) to reduce false-5xx noise while we remedied server-side causes (08:55).

Root cause analysis (hypotheses and evidence):
- Hypothesis A (confirmed primary): periodic KV-cache hot-sweep job executed on an overloaded shard that performed a batch of synchronous KV lease-renew and metadata fetch operations. Those operations took a long tail while contending with normal traffic, which caused acceptor-thread stalls and request queueing at the edge-proxy. Evidence: timing of sweep job + KV latency spikes + acceptor queue sawtooth alignment.
- Hypothesis B (contributing): scheduler coalescing interaction — autoscaler cooldown policy allowed backlog to build then unthrottled, amplifying oscillation. Evidence: scaling policy logs show cooldowns coincident with first two cycles; after moving the sweep to a lower-priority queue, oscillations damped.
- Hypothesis C (unlikely): network flaps — no loss counters or interface errors found in infra metrics.

Final RCA summary:
A scheduled maintenance job (hot-sweep for prefix alignment) executed on shard-12 during a moderately high-traffic window. The job's KV workload performed synchronous lease renewals and metadata fetches that blocked the event loop on several edge-proxy hosts. The blocking caused periodic acceptor queue growth and TTFB spikes as requests queued behind the sweep. Autoscaler cooldown and scaling thresholds allowed the system to oscillate instead of gracefully absorbing the temporary load.

Why the incident was P0:
- Customer-facing latency SLOs breached for multiple tenants.
- Streaming clients experienced visible timeouts and 5xxs.
- High-impact tenants escalated to AMs.

Follow-ups and action items (owner — due):
- Convert hot-sweep to asynchronous, non-blocking implementation (Rajiv Kapoor — 2026-06-04).
- Add guardrails to scheduler so sweep jobs avoid primary serving shards during high-load windows (Aisha Patel — 2026-05-20).
- Update autoscaler cooldown heuristics to consider event-loop stall signals as a throttle trigger (Emma Chen — 2026-05-28).
- Add dashboard panels for acceptor queue distribution per host and overlay with KV-lease latency (Tomás Rivera — 2026-05-18).
- Create a synthetic probe that runs a low-overhead KV operation concurrent with streaming probes to detect sweep-like contention earlier (Emma Chen — 2026-05-25).
- Run a post-deployment chaos test for sweep jobs in staging and validate non-blocking behavior (Eng QA — 2026-06-11).

Runbook updates proposed (quick draft):
- Pre-emptive checks: before scheduling hot-sweep jobs, verify percentiles for event-loop latency and acceptor queue are under thresholds for 10 minutes.
- If TTFB p95 > 1s and acceptor queue grows on >10% hosts: immediately demote running maintenance jobs and notify oncall_sre channel.
- Add a command to quickly identify and pause sweep jobs: /infra pause-sweep --shard <id> (needs script + RBAC).

Oncall play notes (for future responders):
- Don’t immediately scale up acceptor threads globally; target specific hosts and root cause first (sweeps, KV contended ops).
- Use the KV-lease latency heatmap to find sweep-correlated hosts (start with hosts showing >50ms median).
- If disabling sweep is not possible, use traffic re-routing to shift small percentages of traffic off affected hosts to avoid client timeouts.

Commands and dashboards referenced (helpful for next oncall):
- dashboards/hostedapi/ttfb-region-p95
- dashboards/edge/acceptor-queue-length
- infra/kv/lease-latency-heatmap
- infra/scripts/pause-sweep.sh --shard shard-12
- k8s: kubectl -n edge-proxy logs -l app=edge-proxy --since=30m | grep "acceptor-queue"

Notes to self / open questions:
- Need to audit other scheduled jobs with synchronous KV ops — how many use blocking patterns? (Action: Rajiv to inventory by 2026-05-19).
- Why did only a subset of edge hosts show strong acceptor-blocking? Candidate: non-uniform cache hotness due to prefix skew. Plan: run heatmap of prefix keys to hosts.
- Long-term: consider moving lease renewals off critical path entirely.

Post-incident comfort level:
- Confidence that root cause is identified: high (evidence tie-ins).
- Confidence in mitigations: medium — disabling sweep is a stopgap; we need code-level change for full fix.

Appendix (raw notes captured during incident):
- 08:21 "acceptorQ host-03 spiked to 680, KV-lease 320ms" (Tomás)
- 08:24 "scaled threads host-03 -> +50% threadpool, tail q fell but cycles continued" (Emma)
- 08:39 "disabled sweep on shard-12, immediate p95 drop seen on hosts 02/03/07" (Aisha)
- Link: quick summary posted to #oncall_sre: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/GC12345/p1620345600000

Draft status / next steps:
- Marking this doc as a working incident diary. Will convert to formatted postmortem with timeline graphs and aggregated traces once action items are triaged.
- After Rajiv's async refactor lands, schedule a small-scale chaos test to validate non-blocking behaviour.

Unresolved:
- Need to confirm whether autoscaler policy change alone would have prevented oscillation; create simulation ticket (JIRA-SRE-2025).

If you find additional correlations while digging into backend logs, paste into this doc under "Appendix: extra traces".

— Emma C.
